title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array: binary search checking which half is sorted.
shortTitle: Search in Rotated Sorted Array: Binary Search Checking Which Half Is Sorted
keyPoints: In a rotated sorted array split at any mid, at least one half is always properly sorted.
Detect the sorted half by comparing a[left] to a[mid]: if a[left] <= a[mid], the left half is sorted.
Check whether the target falls within the sorted half's range to decide which half to keep.
Use inclusive bounds on the sorted end and exclusive on mid (already checked for equality) to avoid double-counting.
For duplicates, nudge left inward when a[left] == a[mid] == a[right] to resolve ambiguity, accepting O(n) worst case.
The algorithm runs in O(log n) time for distinct elements and O(1) space.
Return -1 when the target is not found after the pointers converge.

s1_definition.oneliner: One half around the middle is always sorted, so check if the target fits in it and keep that half.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Search in Rotated Sorted Array** – finds the index of a target value in a sorted array rotated at one pivot, in O(log n) time.
- **Sorted-half detection** – at any split, compare `a[left]` to `a[mid]` to identify which half is properly sorted.
- **Range check** – if the target lies within the sorted half's range, search there; otherwise search the other half.
- **O(log n) time, O(1) space** – each iteration discards half the remaining elements.
- **Not-found path** – if the pointers converge without finding the target, return `-1`.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has rotated interest-rate checkpoints and an auditor needs to find the exact position of a specific rate. Looking at the middle checkpoint, the auditor notices that one side is still in perfect ascending order. If the target rate falls inside that orderly side's range, search there; otherwise the target must be on the messy side. Each look halves the remaining checkpoints.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│    Search in Rotated Sorted Array Decision Tree     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                     │
│  a[mid] == target?  ──YES──→  Return mid            │
│       │ NO                                          │
│       ▼                                             │
│  a[left] <= a[mid]?                                 │
│    YES → Left half sorted                           │
│       │  target in [a[left], a[mid])?               │
│       │    YES → hi = mid - 1                       │
│       │    NO  → lo = mid + 1                       │
│    NO → Right half sorted                           │
│       │  target in (a[mid], a[right]]?              │
│       │    YES → lo = mid + 1                       │
│       │    NO  → hi = mid - 1                       │
│                                                     │
│  Loop until lo > hi → return -1 (not found)         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Search in Rotated Sorted Array finds the index of a target in a sorted array that has been rotated at one pivot, and you solve it with binary search in O(log n) time and O(1) space. The key observation is that when you split a rotated array at any middle index, at least one half is always properly sorted, so at each step you detect which half is sorted and use a precise range test to decide whether the target lives there.

Concretely, if the left element is less than or equal to the middle, the left half is sorted, and you check whether the target is at least the left value and strictly below the middle; if so you keep the left half, otherwise the right. If the left is greater than the middle, the right half is sorted and you do the symmetric check. Identifying the sorted half is what lets ordinary range reasoning work despite the rotation.

The part that catches people is the inclusive and exclusive boundaries. You use inclusive bounds on the sorted end and exclusive bounds at the middle so the middle element, which you already tested for equality, is never considered twice, and you use less-than-or-equal when comparing left to middle so two-element windows resolve correctly. For duplicates you nudge the left pointer inward when all three are equal, accepting a linear worst case.

In a banking project at the National Bank of India, this is used on rotated interest-rate checkpoints so an audit feature can find the exact index of a given rate and report cleanly when a rate is absent.

Remember one sentence: Detect which half is sorted, range-check the target against that half, and discard the other half to search a rotated array in O(log n) time.
